intro: Olga Gurevich plays the Waltz in C♯ minor, Op. 64 No. 2, which has three distinct themes: a melody in C♯ minor, quick descending quavers and a slower melody in D♭ major. The running quaver theme returns between the other two.

sections.label: A · Tempo giusto, held notes and flourishes
sections.mNote: Tempo giusto. A chordal melody above the waltz bass.

sections.label: B · Più mosso, descending quavers
sections.mNote: Più mosso; the right hand plays running quavers.

sections.label: C · Più lento in D♭ major
sections.mNote: Più lento: the melody moves at a slower tempo.

sections.label: D · Song melody and returning quavers
sections.mNote: The long melody leads back towards C♯ minor.

sections.label: E · The chordal melody again
sections.mNote: Long notes return between the right hand’s flourishes

sections.label: F · Last return of the quaver refrain
sections.mNote: Descending quavers carry the waltz to its close

cues.title: Opening, Tempo giusto
cues.text: Two notes sound together in the right hand and are held across the bar line, followed by a small, quick curl. Below, the left hand leaps from a bass note to two chords. Chopin marks the opening Tempo giusto.
cues.evidence: Score, opening Tempo giusto; engraving by Knute Snortum (2023), p. 1. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP879636-PMLP2373-waltz-op64-no2.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Più mosso, quaver theme
cues.text: At Più mosso the right hand runs down in chains of quavers while the left hand keeps the bass-and-two-chords pattern. This is the waltz’s recurring tune. It returns after each of the broader melodies.
cues.evidence: Score, first Più mosso, pp. 1–2; its returns appear on pp. 3 and 5. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP879636-PMLP2373-waltz-op64-no2.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Più lento in D♭ major
cues.text: The key signature changes from four sharps to five flats, giving D♭ major, which on the keyboard is the major-key twin of C♯ minor. The marking is Più lento, slower. Long notes in the melody are held above chords that contain short lines of their own in reply.
cues.evidence: Score, Più lento, pp. 2–3: D♭ major key signature and sustained melody. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP879636-PMLP2373-waltz-op64-no2.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Olga Gurevich, Baku to New York
cues.text: As a girl in Baku, Gurevich went from ordinary school to music school, where she had piano lessons and studied solfège, music history and choir. At seventeen she moved to Moscow to study at the Gnesin Academy. In 1998 she settled in New York, where she performs and teaches.
cues.evidence: Childhood and Gnesin training: https://www.bsmny.org/team/olga-gurevich-2/. Move to New York: https://www.musiciansclubofny.org/biographies/olgagurevich

cues.title: Final refrain and close
cues.text: The running refrain returns for the last time. Its quavers fall, climb and fall again over the left hand’s three-beat accompaniment. The waltz ends with a cadence in C♯ minor.
cues.evidence: Score, final Più mosso and C♯ minor cadence, p. 5. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP879636-PMLP2373-waltz-op64-no2.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: Composer for the piano, known for music that drew on operatic singing and on the irregular accents of the mazurka.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832 Chopin, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist, played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. He had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers, and teaching soon supplied his living. For the rest of his life his profession depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from one concert city to the next; Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. The family moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
